entities.name: Marcellus of Tangier
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Marcellus of Tangier, also known as Marcellus the Centurion, was a Roman centurion executed on October 30, 298 CE, in Tingis (modern Tangier, Morocco), under the reign of Emperor Maximian Herculius. His refusal to participate in pagan rituals and his public renunciation of military service due to his Christian faith positioned him as a prominent martyr during the nascent stages of the Diocletianic Persecution, a period of intense state-sponsored suppression against Christianity. His story highlights the profound conflict between imperial Roman authority and the burgeoning Christian identity, making him a significant figure in early Christian hagiography and a venerated saint in both Eastern Orthodox and Catholic traditions.

Marcellus served as a centurion in the Legio Ioviana, stationed in Tingis. The pivotal event occurred during the celebration of Emperor Maximian's birthday, a compulsory public festival involving pagan sacrifices and idolatry. On July 28, 298 CE, Marcellus publicly cast off his military insignia and declared, 'I serve Jesus Christ the eternal King, and I despise your emperors.' This act, a direct defiance of imperial religious policy and military oath, led to his immediate arrest. He was subsequently tried before the vicarius Fortunatus in Tingis and later before the deputy prefect Aurelius Agricolanus in León (Legio VII Gemina), where he steadfastly affirmed his Christian faith and his refusal to serve in a pagan army. He was condemned for desertion and impiety and beheaded.
